title: The Little Albert Experiment: The Perverse 1920 Study That Made a Baby Afraid of Santa Claus & Bunnies
description:
in History, Psychology, Science |   	September 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The field of psy­chol­o­gy is very dif­fer­ent than it used to
body:
in History, Psychology, Science |   	September 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

The field of psy­chol­o­gy is very dif­fer­ent than it used to be. Nowa­days, the Amer­i­can Psy­cho­log­i­cal Asso­ci­a­tion has a code of con­duct for exper­i­ments that ensures a subject’s con­fi­den­tial­i­ty, consent,and gen­er­al men­tal well-being. In the old days, it was­n’t the case.
Back then, you could, for instance, con sub­jects into think­ing that they were elec­tro­cut­ing a man to death, as they did in the infa­mous 1961 Mil­gram exper­i­ment, which left peo­ple trau­ma­tized and hum­bled in the knowl­edge that deep down they are lit­tle more than weak-willed pup­pets in the face of author­i­ty. You could also try to turn a group of unsus­pect­ing orphans into stut­ter­ers by method­i­cal­ly under­min­ing their self-esteem as the folks who ran the apt­ly named Mon­ster Study of 1939 tried to do. But, if you real­ly want to get into the swamp of moral dubi­ous­ness, look no fur­ther than the Lit­tle Albert exper­i­ments, which trau­ma­tized a baby into hat­ing dogs, San­ta Claus, and all things fuzzy.

In 1920, Johns Hop­kins pro­fes­sor John B. Wat­son was fas­ci­nat­ed with Ivan Pavlov’s research on con­di­tioned stim­u­lus. Pavlov famous­ly rang a bell every time he fed his dogs. At first the food caused the dogs to sali­vate, but after a spell of pair­ing the bell with din­ner, the dogs would even­tu­al­ly sali­vate at just the sound of the bell. That’s called a con­di­tioned response. Wat­son want­ed to see if he could cre­ate a con­di­tioned response in a baby.
Enter 9‑month-old Albert B., AKA Lit­tle Albert. At the begin­ning of the exper­i­ment, Albert was pre­sent­ed with a white rat, a dog, a white rab­bit, and a mask of San­ta Claus among oth­er things. The lad was unafraid of every­thing and was, in fact, real­ly tak­en with the rat. Then every time the baby touched the ani­mals, sci­en­tists struck a met­al bar behind him, cre­at­ing a star­tling­ly loud bang. The sound freaked out the child and soon, like Pavlov’s dogs, Lit­tle Albert grew ter­ri­fied of the rat and the mask of San­ta and even a fur coat. The par­tic­u­lar­ly messed up thing about the exper­i­ment was that Wat­son didn’t even both­er to reverse the psy­cho­log­i­cal trau­ma he inflict­ed.

What hap­pened to poor baby Albert is hard to say, in part because no one is real­ly sure of the child’s true iden­ti­ty. He might have been Dou­glas Mer­ritte, as psy­chol­o­gists Hall P. Beck and Shar­man Levin­son argued in 2009. If that’s the case, then the child died at the age of 6 in 1925 of hydro­cephalus. Or he might have been William Albert Barg­er, as Russ Pow­ell and Nan­cy Dig­don argued in 2012. He passed away in 2007 at the age of 87. He report­ed­ly had a life­long aver­sion to dogs, though it can­not be deter­mined if it was a last­ing effect of the exper­i­ment.
Lat­er in life, Wat­son left aca­d­e­mi­cia for adver­tis­ing. You can watch a video of the exper­i­ment above.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
Watch Footage from the Psy­chol­o­gy Exper­i­ment That Shocked the World: Milgram’s Obe­di­ence Study (1961)
The Pow­er of Con­for­mi­ty: 1962 Episode of Can­did Cam­era Reveals the Strange Psy­chol­o­gy of Rid­ing Ele­va­tors
Her­mann Rorschach’s Orig­i­nal Rorschach Test: What Do You See? (1921)

Jonathan Crow is a writer and film­mak­er whose work has appeared in Yahoo!, The Hol­ly­wood Reporter, and oth­er pub­li­ca­tions.

title: Read the CIA’s Manual of Trickery and Deception, Written by a Professional Stage Magician
description:
in Books, History |   	September 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in Books, History |   	September 28th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
The idea of a young­ster vac­il­lat­ing between whether to become a magi­cian or join the Cen­tral Intel­li­gence Agency may sound implau­si­ble, but those two work­ing envi­ron­ments have deep­er com­mon­al­i­ties than it would seem. So, in any case, believes John McLaugh­lin, whose more than 30 years at the CIA includ­ed peri­ods as its deputy direc­tor and act­ing direc­tor. He also describes him­self as a life­long ama­teur magi­cian, an avo­ca­tion that owes much to his boy­hood dis­cov­ery of Quick­er Than the Eye, a mag­ic man­u­al from 1932 by one John Mul­hol­land. Around the same time the young McLaugh­lin came across that book in the library, Mul­hol­land was writ­ing the more spe­cial­ized guide­books Some Oper­a­tional Appli­ca­tions of the Art of Decep­tion and Recog­ni­tion Sig­nals — though nobody with­out a seri­ous secu­ri­ty clear­ance would have known it.
In 1953, Mul­hol­land left his posi­tion as edi­tor of the magi­cians’ trade mag­a­zine The Sphinx, osten­si­bly for health rea­sons, but actu­al­ly to go to work for the CIA. Formed just six years before, the orga­ni­za­tion was still deter­min­ing what its mis­sion of pre­vent­ing sur­prise for­eign attacks against the U.S. and coun­ter­ing the glob­al advance of com­mu­nism would entail on the ground. To any­one who’s made enough of a habit of nov­els and films deal­ing with Cold War espi­onage, it may come as no sur­prise that the arts of dis­guise, mis­di­rec­tion, and sleight of hand prac­ticed by mas­ter magi­cians would look use­ful indeed to the CIA. “Just as a magician’s meth­ods must elude detec­tion in front of a close­ly atten­tive audi­ence,” writes McLaugh­lin, “so an intel­li­gence offi­cer doing espi­onage work must elude close sur­veil­lance and pass mes­sages and materiel with­out detec­tion.”
Addi­tion­al­ly, “ana­lysts must be as famil­iar as magi­cians with meth­ods of decep­tion, because ana­lysts are almost always work­ing with incom­plete infor­ma­tion and in cir­cum­stances where an adver­sary is seek­ing to mis­lead them — or in the magician’s term, mis­di­rect them.” The Com­pa­ny’s spe­cial­ists in coun­ter­in­tel­li­gence described their sub­field as a “wilder­ness of mir­rors,” an expres­sion pro­fes­sion­al illu­sion­ists must find espe­cial­ly evoca­tive. Com­mis­sioned in the time of the CIA’s human-exper­i­men­ta­tion pro­gram MKULTRA, pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture, Mul­hol­land’s man­u­als were long assumed offi­cial­ly destroyed along with many oth­er of its doc­u­ments in 1973. After they unex­pect­ed­ly resur­faced dur­ing declas­si­fi­ca­tion in the two-thou­sands, they were pub­lished in The Offi­cial CIA Man­u­al of Trick­ery and Decep­tion by Agency his­to­ri­ans H. Kei­th Melton and Robert Wal­lace. You can find a copy over at the Inter­net Archive.
At that time, the Boston Globe pub­lished illus­trat­ed expla­na­tions of some of Mul­hol­land’s tech­niques, such as trans­port­ing spies using a mech­a­nism sim­i­lar to the one that con­ceals an appar­ent­ly sawed-in-half stage­hand, or sur­rep­ti­tious­ly drop­ping into a drink a pill affixed to the back of a book of match­es. Amid “the super­pow­er strug­gle for pow­er and influ­ence around the world,” writes Tom Scoc­ca, “both the ideas and tech­niques of secret war per­vad­ed the cul­ture — the cor­ro­sive belief in hid­den con­spir­a­cy and the nifty thrill of spy­craft itself, the codes and dis­guis­es and minia­ture cam­eras.” Today, “Mulholland’s account of real-world stage­craft amounts to an eti­quette man­u­al for a lost moment of his­to­ry. The match­book trick depends on peo­ple smok­ing and drink­ing. There is a sur­vey of the many pock­ets found in every man’s suit, and which ones are most nat­ur­al for casu­al­ly slip­ping objects into.” How­ev­er much of the romance has drained out of espi­onage — as it has from so much else since the mid-twen­ti­eth cen­tu­ry — the best magi­cians know that old tricks can always be re-enchant­ed for a new world. You can read The Offi­cial CIA Man­u­al of Trick­ery and Decep­tion here.
Relat­ed con­tent:
12 Mil­lion Declas­si­fied CIA Doc­u­ments Now Free Online: Secret Tun­nels, UFOs, Psy­chic Exper­i­ments & More
Dis­cov­er the CIA’s Sim­ple Sab­o­tage Field Man­u­al: A Time­less Guide to Sub­vert­ing Any Orga­ni­za­tion with “Pur­pose­ful Stu­pid­i­ty” (1944)
The CIA’s For­mer Chief of Dis­guise Show How Spies Use Cos­tumes in Under­cov­er Oper­a­tions
Inside MKUl­tra, the CIA’s Secret Pro­gram That Used LSD to Achieve Mind Con­trol (1953–1973)
When the CIA Stud­ied Psy­chic Tech­niques to Alter Human Con­scious­ness & Unlock Time Trav­el: Dis­cov­er “The Gate­way Process”
The CIA’s Rec­tal Tool Kit for Spies — Cre­at­ed for Tru­ly Des­per­ate Sit­u­a­tions Dur­ing The Cold War
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: A Giant Gold Coil by Plastique Fantastique Created a Loopy Portal on the High Line
description: Earlier this month, a monumental, metallic spiral appeared on the High Line to coincide with New York Fashion Week. The elevated, art-filled publi
body:
Earlier this month, a monumental, metallic spiral appeared on the High Line to coincide with New York Fashion Week. The elevated, art-filled public park on the West Side of Manhattan runs from Gansevoort Street near the Whitney Museum of American Art to 34th Street near Hudson Yards. Commissioned by Bulgari as part of its Serpenti Infinito series, which celebrates its famous Serpenti collection through artistic partnerships, the temporary installation invited visitors to walk through an enormous coil titled “auroBOROS: Urban Memory and Collective Dream.”
The brainchild of artists Marco Canevacci and Yena Young, who helm the studio Plastique Fantastique, “auroBOROS” spent nearly two weeks wedged beneath a raised building. Its title is drawn from the ancient ouroboros motif of a snake eating its own tail as a metaphor for the continuous cycles of life—a nod to Bulgari’s snake-themed jewelry line—and the site added a playful tension to the piece, as it appeared to support the overhead structure.

“auroBOROS” marks the first time Plastique Fantastique has exhibited in the U.S. Earlier installations along a similar theme include iterations of an architectonic gold loop titled “RINGdeLUXE,” which has encircled bridges with the appearance of a kind of cosmic portal. See more on the studio’s Instagram.


“RINGdeLUXE” (2023)

title: At a 'Molecular Level,' Mu Pan Composes Meticulous Mandalas in Acrylic
description: In the Buddhist tradition, mandalas are devotional images that represent the universe, their precise geometry and motifs depicting holy realms and
body:
In the Buddhist tradition, mandalas are devotional images that represent the universe, their precise geometry and motifs depicting holy realms and a sense of order through symbolic references to the elements and astrology. Tibetan Buddhist monks painstakingly create colorful sand renditions as part of their mindfulness practice. Once complete, the pieces are ritualistically destroyed—the sand is customarily returned to moving water—to illustrate the impermanence and transience of life and the cosmos.
For artist Mu Pan, the mandala inspires the foundation of a series of vivid works on paper. In his current solo exhibition, Micro MUniverse at Hashimoto Contemporary, the Brooklyn-based artist composes explosive, eccentric, narrative scenes rendered at what the gallery describes as “a molecular level.” 
“18 Angels” (2026), acrylic on paper, 7 1/2 x 7 1/2 inches
The collection draws on a Chinese Buddhist adage that a single cup of water contains countless lifeforms, and for that reason, care must be taken in consuming it. Mu delves into a world of fantasy and symmetry, where animals, humans, and plants converge and hybridize in surreal configurations. Some become nearly abstract; others are uncanny, even slightly grotesque. The figures are at turns ecstatic, devious, and serene: black-winged skeletons meet sublime beings in “18 Angels,” and a dramatic scene of woodland creatures divinely erupts in “Burning Rabbit.”
Many of the works are less than a foot wide, with the exception of one painting on panel called “4 Brutes” that’s two feet across. Line, form, and expressions are therefore composed in incredible detail. The artist says, “I want to focus on the concept of being small, because whatever is small actually contains way more than it appears. Therefore, each small image is like a drop of blood, and each drop of blood contains multiple universes.”
Micro MUniverse continues through October 10 in New York City. See more on the artist’s Instagram. 
“Burning Rabbit” (2026), acrylic on paper, 7 3/4 x 7 inches
“4 Brutes” (2026), acrylic on wood panel, 20 x 24 inches
“Deer” (2026), acrylic on paper, 15 x 10 3/4 inches
“Purple Weasel” (2026, acrylic on paper, 15 x 11 inches
“Green” (2026), acrylic on paper, 14 3/4 x 14 3/4 inches
“Bear” (2026), acrylic on paper, 15 x 13 inches

title: October 2026 Opportunities: Open Calls, Residencies, and Grants for Artists
description: Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never mis
body:
Every month, we share opportunities for artists and designers, including open calls, grants, fellowships, and residencies. Make sure you never miss out by joining our monthly Opportunities Newsletter.
Arch Enemy Arts Call for ArtistsFeaturedArch Enemy Arts is seeking submissions for an annual group exhibition in January 2027. This spotlight exhibition of new and emerging talent has no themes or direction in subject matter, although the gallery focuses on representational, dark surrealism, magical realism, post-graffiti, pop-surrealism, narrative, illustrative, and figurative work across a range of artistic mediums. The exhibition is open to artists worldwide, who are invited to submit up to three works for consideration.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EST on November 13, 2026.
$4,500 Artist GrantsFeaturedThe Hopper Prize is now accepting entries for $4,500 and $1,000 artist grants from a total pool of $13,000. Two artists will each receive $4,500 and four artists will each receive $1,000. This is an international open call, and all visual media is eligible. The Hopper Prize provides a direct path to get your work in front of an international community of curators, artists, gallerists, and arts administrators. Additional exposure is available via a 30 artist shortlist, an online journal, and an Instagram account currently reaching over 175,000.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PST on November 17, 2026.
Open Calls
Black Public Media Open Call for Documentaries(U.S.)Independent filmmakers are invited to submit feature-length nonfiction projects in a range of formats, styles, subject matters, and genres for the opportunity to participate in the 10th PitchBLACK Forum & Awards next spring. BPM is particularly interested in stories exploring critical issues, promoting cultural understanding, and engaging national audiences and/or local communities. All projects, which may be in pre-production, production, or early post-production, must be suitable for public media distribution.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. PDT on October 1, 2026.
American Color Print Society 86th Annual Fall Exhibition(U.S.)For 86 years, the American Color Print Society has been dedicated to the advancement of printmaking as a fine art medium. This opportunity is open both members and non-members, and all accepted artists are eligible for awards. There is a $45 application fee for non-members ($20 for members).Deadline: October 1, 2026.
The Defiance Award(Australia)This prize was founded to discover, support, and profile exceptional Australian painters. It offers both financial support and professional development opportunities to foster long-term careers in the arts, ensuring artists are equipped to thrive and grow within their practice. The overall winner will receive a solo exhibition at Defiance Gallery, a two-week residency at Giverny Artist Residency in Queenstown, New Zealand, sponsored by the Nock Art Foundation, return flights to Queenstown from an Australian capital city, and $5,000 cash.Deadline: October 7, 2026.
Royal Institute of Oil Painters Annual Exhibition(International)Artists are invited to submit work for the ROI Annual Exhibition 2026. Founded in 1882, ROI is the only major British art society that promotes and exhibits work of the highest standard exclusively in oil paint. The ROI welcomes submissions on all subjects and approaches to the medium, and this year’s optional theme is “winter rituals.” There’s a submission fee of £22 per work, or £14.50 per work for artists aged 35 or under.Deadline: 12 p.m. BST on October 9, 2026.
MAKE Commercial Workshop(International)MAKE’s Commercial Workshop gives junior and senior BFA/BA students an immersive, hands-on experience in creating animated commercial spots. Across two semesters, selected teams collaborate with MAKE mentors to conceptualize, design, and produce a 15-second, character-driven ad. The workshop mirrors the pace and challenges of MAKE’s studio projects, helping students sharpen their skills, build their portfolios, and gain real-world insight into commercial animation.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on October 11, 2026.
YICCA Art Prize(International)This competition is open to all media and techniques and geared toward emerging artists, with a total prize pool of €5,500. The application fee varies depending on the number of images submitted and starts at €50.Deadline: October 8, 2026.
2027 ArtFields Festival(Southeastern U.S.)Submit to the 2027 ArtFields Festival and be part of a unique celebration of art and community in Lake City, South Carolina. Selected artworks will be in one of the Southeast’s largest and most prestigious art events from April 9 to May 1, 2027, and will be in the running for over $100,000 in cash prizes. There is a $25 application fee.Deadline: November 1, 2026.
2027 Beam Camp Project Open Call(International)Beam Center, located in Strafford, New Hampshire, seeks design proposals for an ambitious public artwork that will be brought to life through collaborations between youth, Beam Camp staff, and the selected proposer. Projects will be realized by a community of more than 100 young people at Beam Camp in July 2026. Selected project proposers receive a $5,000 award, and selected projects have approximately a $15,000 fabrication budget.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EST on November 30, 2026.
Material Works Art Award 2026(International)Material Works supports artists through one-time $2,500 awards in exchange for original pieces added to its growing contemporary art collection. The award recognizes artistic excellence and aims to promote career advancement through increasing visibility and exposure. There is a €40 application fee.Deadline: December 6, 2026, or when the first 300 artworks submitted, whichever comes first.
Grants
The Supporting Act Foundation Artist Grants(Europe)The Supporting Act Foundation offers 10 unrestricted grants of €10,000 each, paid in monthly installments of €1,000. The program aims to improve living conditions for artists, enabling them to dedicate more time to developing their practices. To be eligible, artists must be based in Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, or the U.K.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
New York City Film Production Grant(New York City)This grant supports eligible New York City-based early career film directors whose work takes creative risks in expanding, questioning, experimenting with, or re-imagining filmmaking with production grants of up to $30,000.Deadline: 4 p.m. EDT on October 1, 2026.
Printed Matter Publisher Work Grant(International)In its third year, Printed Matter’s Publisher Work Grant program offers funding to independent presses with a history of artists’ book publishing, acknowledging awardees’ accomplishments in past work and providing the capacity-building funds to enable future book projects and publisher sustainability. In 2026, three unrestricted grants of $10,000 will be awarded to three independent artists’ book publishers. Printed Matter will also extend a featured exhibitor presence at a forthcoming Printed Matter NY or LA Art Book Fair to selected presses.Deadline: October 4, 2026.
The Meridian Award(International)The Meridian Award is an independent international award granting a $1,000 unrestricted cash prize to one contemporary artist working in any medium. ​Founded independently in New York City, the award supports independent, self-directed contemporary practices and welcomes submissions from artists worldwide.​ There is a $25 application fee.Deadline: October 15, 2026.
Oklahoma Visual Arts Coalition Grants for Artists (Oklahoma)OVAC offers several opportunities, including the Grants for Artists program fostering Oklahoma’s visual artistic creative excellence and the Community/Artist Partnership grants, which provide up to $1,500 for initiating community-based projects that lead to artwork creation. Creative Projects grants provide up to $1,500 for creating new work that will culminate in a public event focused on artist’s own work. Two additional grants are available in Education Assistance and Professional Basics categories, amounting $500 each.Deadline: October 15, 2026.
MAKE Animation Thesis Grants(International)MAKE is proud to continue its annual grant program supporting senior animation students around the globe, championing and spotlighting emerging talent by directly funding original animated thesis projects (short films). First place is $2,000; second place is $1,000, and third place is $500.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EST on November 6, 2026.
Asian Cultural Counsel Grants(Asia)ACC supports artists, scholars, arts professionals, and organizations through fellowships and grants that advance cultural exchange between the U.S. and Asia and within Asia. For individuals, the organization offers the six-month New York Fellowship, the one- to six-month Individual Fellowship, and the Graduate Fellowship for a student from Asia to study in the U.S.Deadline: 9:59 a.m. EST on November 10, 2026.
The Adolf and Esther Gottlieb Emergency Grant (International)This program provides one-time financial assistance to qualified painters, printmakers, and sculptors whose needs resulted from an unforeseen catastrophic incident and who lack the resources to meet that situation. Awardees typically receive $5,000 and up to $15,000.Deadline: Rolling.
Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant (International)The foundation welcomes applications from painters, sculptors, and artists working on paper, including printmakers. Grants are intended for one year and range up to $50,000. The artist’s circumstances determine the size of the grant, and professional exhibition history will be considered.Deadline: Rolling.
Residencies, Fellowships, & More
Art Omi Dance, Music, and Architecture Residencies(International)Art Omi is currently offering residencies in three tracks: architecture, dance, and music. The program  nurtures experimentation in environs that offer a singular blend of rural quiet and cultural stimulation, while tapping into the freedom to play through collaboration. There is a $15 application fee.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
Lighthouse Works Fellowship(International)Located on Fishers Island, New York, Lighthouse Works offers a fellowship supporting a diverse range of cultural producers working in the vanguard of their creative fields. Fellowships are six weeks in length, occur year-round, and provide fellows with housing, food, studio space, and $1,750 in financial support. Fellows enjoy a private bedroom and share a kitchen, bathrooms, and living space in a three-story Victorian house. All dietary needs are accommodated, and on most nights, Lighthouse Works staff cook for and eat dinner with the fellows. Studios are located about 1.5 miles/a 30-minute walk from the fellowship house. The application fee is $25.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
Woodson Art Museum Glass Box Studio Residency(International)Located on the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum campus in Wausau, Wisconsin, the Glass Box Studio provides space and time for artists to experiment, explore, and produce individually developed or collaborative artwork in any medium. Participating artists will receive an honorarium in addition to reimbursement for travel, mileage, and meal expenses. Supplies and materials for workshops, classes, and outreach will be covered by the Woodson Art Museum. There is a $25 application fee.Deadline: October 1, 2026.
Abrons Art Center Visual Artist AIRspace Residency(New York City)Abrons Art Center supports a cohort of three visual artists for a 20-month residency. Each fellow will be paired with a professional artist mentor who is an alum of the program and will support the fellows’ creative and professional development. Artists receive a semi-private studio, an annual honorarium of $7,000, an annual materials stipend of $5,000, and more.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on October 4, 2026.
Pedantic Summer and Fall 2027 Residencies(International)Pedantic Arts is seeking applicants for creatives and researchers to participate in the Summer 2027 and Fall 2027 Terms. Entering its sixth year, Pedantic continues its mission of re-embracing the impact that education, study, and contemplation can have on artistic output by interconnecting creators, organizers, and critics. Residents will spend four weeks housed in a hybrid residential and commercial building in the bustling Pittsburgh’s Garfield neighborhood. Two Pedantic Research Grant opportunities, which encompass one- to two-week-long independent research stays in Pittsburgh, are also open through the same application process. There is a $20 application fee.Deadline: 11:59 p.m. EDT on October 15, 2026.
Leighton Artist Studio Residencies at Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity(International)For program dates between April 5, 2027, and March 31, 2028, Banff Centre of Arts and Creativity invites applications for three Leighton Artist Studio Residency opportunities: solo, group, and photography. Residencies run for a minimum of two weeks and up to six weeks long, and each resident has a meal plan, housing, studio space, and access to campus facilities, including the library. Scholarships may be available. There is a $65 application fee for individuals, or $35 for applicants who identify as Indigenous.Deadline: October 14, 2026.
The Center for Art & Advocacy’s Center Fellowship(U.S.)The Center Fellowship (formerly Right of Return) offers an annual award of $10,000 in unrestricted funds and $10,000 in project development funds to formerly incarcerated artists. Fellows are invited to an annual retreat to network with previous fellows, advocates, industry leaders, and funders. The Center Fellowship is open to any directly justice-impacted, U.S.-based artist working in visual art, film, music, creative writing, performance, design, or other multidisciplinary practice, regardless of citizenship status, felony convictions, or formal training in the arts.Deadline: October 25, 2026.
The Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowship for Immigrant Artists(U.S.)Each year, The Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowship selects 30 fellows based on their potential to make significant contributions to American society, culture, and their chosen fields. The program provides $90,000 over the course of two years to support graduate study. Fellows may be immigrants or the children of immigrants and receive funding along with mentorship, community, and lifelong connection to a network of nearly 900 Fellows across various disciplines including the arts.Deadline: 2 p.m. EDT on October 29, 2026.
Vital Impacts Environmental Photography Fellowships and Mentorships(International)Vital Impacts is dedicated to supporting visual storytellers who capture compelling, solutions-focused environmental stories at the local level. The organization is offering one $20,000 fellowship and six $5,000 fellowships to help bring these vital stories to life. Recipients will have twelve months to develop their projects with support from Vital Impacts to publish and showcase their work. Additionally, ten emerging photographers will be chosen to participate in an intensive mentorship program, designed to nurture their growth and enhance their craft.Deadline: November 30, 2026.
Roger Tory Peterson Institute Artist-in-Residence(International)Residents spend a week at the Roger Tory Peterson Institute (RTPI) in Jamestown, New York, with facilitated access to the Peterson Collection, inclusive of Roger’s original field guide art, fine art, films, slides and personal papers. Each artist receives an honorarium of $1,000. Artists from out of town also receive housing, per diem, and reimbursement for travel. Following the residency, artists create a body of work inspired by their time spent at RTPI, which is featured in a solo exhibition the following year.Deadline: Rolling.
Quarantine (International)Dubbed “purgatory for artists,” Quarantine is a week-long intensive art program on an 18th-century quarantine island off the coast of Menorca, Spain. The program is open to beginners and professionals alike and offers three 45-minute private mentorships throughout the week, with activities lasting 12+ hours per day. Phones are banned.Deadline: Rolling.

body:
Feature
                Two exhibitions at the Puffin Foundation Center chronicle 250 years of organizing, social movements, and civic engagement in the city.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            An installation view of the “Direct Action” section of Raise Your Voice: New York Activism at the Museum of the City of New York (all photos Rhea Nayyar/Hyperallergic unless otherwise noted)
    
        
            Marches, megaphones, and messaging are activism's most visible components in this day and age, but they're certainly not the only way to get involved in changing one's community for the better. The Museum of the City of New York's (MCNY) newest permanent exhibit identifies the ingredients of a successful movement and highlights some bite-sized starting points for civic engagement for visitors at any stage.Opening today, September 25, Raise Your Voice marks one of two inaugural exhibitions in MCNY's new Puffin Foundation Center for New York City Activism — the culmination of a multimillion-dollar gift from the nonprofit devoted to uplifting minority artists and organizations. Curated by Sarah Seidman, Raise Your Voice emerges from the framework of its longstanding predecessor, Activist New York (2014–2026), which explored how the city's population density, diversity, and class disparity were critical for hundreds of social and economic movements that yielded nationwide impacts.Entrance for Raise Your VoiceSeidman, who was appointed as the curator of social activism at MCNY shortly after Activist New York opened, noted that the original display had rotating material and was the most-visited exhibition among school groups. But as an update, Seidman said that Raise Your Voice and its place in the broader Puffin Foundation Center are more interactive and hands-on, “which really reflects the direction and top priorities of the museum.”Raise Your Voice distills activism into five main components. “Demonstrations,” “Organizing,” “Arts & Media,” and “Direct Action” examine how frontline, behind-the-scenes, supplemental, and extrajudicial labor coalesce to advance social change, while a final section called “Your City, Your Move” equips visitors with tangible means of instituting change on a local level.

title: Activists Unveil Quilt Honoring Thousands Disappeared by ICE in Minnesota
description:

                The Stolen Neighbors Quilt features 11,000 hand-stitched squares in an indictment of violence against immig
body:
News
                The Stolen Neighbors Quilt features 11,000 hand-stitched squares in an indictment of violence against immigrants and a “call for political courage.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Protestors unfurl the "Stolen Neighbors Quilt" in the Minnesota State Capitol Rotunda on September 22, 2026. (photo courtesy Minnesota Immigrant Rights Action Committee)
    
        
            Activists unfurled a 24-foot-long quilt protesting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence at the Minnesota State Capitol on Tuesday, September 22. Made of 11,000 individual patches representing individuals disappeared by ICE in the state, the “Stolen Neighbors” quilt was stitched together by dozens of volunteers over the course of five months.MIRAC member Owen Lubozynski told Hyperallergic that he was inspired to create the quilt based on discussions with activists about the most effective ways to keep people, including key Minnesotan lawmakers, engaged after Operation Metro Surge, President Trump’s deadly deployment of more than 3,000 Minnesotan officers and ICE agents across the state this past year. ICE agents shot three people; Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti were murdered on camera while protesting ICE presence in the Twin Cities. Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan immigrant, was shot in the leg, but survived. “We wanted to resist a return to normalcy while Minnesotans were still being quietly terrorized,” Lubozynski told Hyperallergic. “I thought one way to do that would be to create a visual representation of every stolen neighbor, one that was impossible to ignore.” Protestors carry the heavy "Stolen Neighbors Quilt" around the central insignia in the Minnesota State Capitol Rotunda. (photo courtesy Minnesota Immigrant Rights Action Committee)Although they originally intended to unveil the quilt over the mezzanine, members of the Minnesota Immigrant Rights Action Committee (MIRAC) realized it was too long and might hit some light fixtures, so once inside the Capitol, they slowly unfolded the quilt horizontally over the rotunda floor as they chanted “stand up, fight back.” A few representatives looked on from the balcony above as supporters in inflatable frog suits stood around in solidarity.
